chapter: Civil service, Keyhole club and civil rights
title: Picketing and integrating the Texas military bases
summary: Albert says he walked picket lines at big stores and, using officer contacts, helped integrate bases through the Goodwill Society.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: I was also responsible for integrating most of the bases because I fought the civil rights here. I picketed the Jaskis, walked the pickets, the biggest store in the state of Texas. The handy andy stores, the biggest chain stores in the state of Texas. I walked the picket line. What about all of these things? Now, what I'm referring to on the walking in the pickets lines now is in 1950, 2053. The Keough case was in 52. The bases recently, about six years ago, was at Randolph when I had an investigation from the old school. In 1941, I organized the first Goodwill Society for the benefit of the Negroes at Kennedy.
How did that Goodwill Society work? Actually, I don't know anything about that anymore.

Well, I had the privilege, being a foeman, of going into the higher up of the brackets, meeting the colonels. And then too, I played a little music then, and I would meet these colonels at the officers' club, and they'd invite me to the table to take a drink with them. And in so drinking, or talking with them, I would tell them the situation that was on the base. So they'd say, well okay, we're having fun tonight. See me Monday morning. Monday morning, I would be in his office, and I would explain to him the situation of the Negroes. So Colonel Hicks, he said, why don't you organize? He said, will you give me the privilege? I said, sure. So I organized with the Negroes that I thought that I could depend on. That was the Goodwill Society for the betterment of the Negroes. That was my name. I had given it to him. So when the Colonel, you know how the army works, I mean, they moved the personnel around me, juggled them like a checkerboard. So this Colonel left, and a southern major took over, and he gradually eased me out of what I was doing, and set up a consular for him. And he put what we call, Uncle Tom Negro in charge. So what I was doing, we went down the drain. That was another reason why I went to leave and open the nightclub. So we get back from one thing to the other.
